content: Deferred gratification, also known as delayed gratification, refers to the ability of an individual to resist the temptation for an immediate reward and wait for a later, often more substantial, reward. This ability is widely regarded as a critical personality trait that contributes significantly to achieving success in life. Daniel Goleman, a prominent psychologist, has emphasized that deferred gratification is a key component of emotional intelligence. Individuals who lack this trait are often described as requiring instant gratification and may exhibit poor impulse control. Psychoanalysts have theorized that poor impulse control is associated with weak ego boundaries. This concept originates from Sigmund Freud's theory of personality, which delineates the id as the pleasure principle, the superego as the morality principle, and the ego as the reality principle. The ego's primary function is to mediate between the id's desires and the superego's moral constraints while considering the needs of others. According to this framework, individuals who struggle to delay gratification may have an overactive id that the ego and superego fail to regulate effectively. Biological factors in the brain may also play a role in poor impulse control. For instance, research has shown that children with fetal alcohol syndrome exhibit a diminished capacity to delay gratification. One of the most well-known studies on this concept is the marshmallow experiment, conducted by Walter Mischel at Stanford University and later discussed by Daniel Goleman in his work. In the 1960s, a group of four-year-old children participated in this experiment. Each child was given a marshmallow and promised a second one if they could refrain from eating the first marshmallow for 20 minutes. Some children successfully waited, while others did not. The researchers tracked the participants into adolescence and found that those who had the ability to delay gratification were better adjusted, more dependable (as reported by their parents and teachers), and scored an average of 210 points higher on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). Another notable test of impulse control is the gift delay experiment. In this test, children were presented with an attractively wrapped gift but were instructed to complete a puzzle before opening it. Researchers calculated a delay score based on how long the children resisted opening the gift. Follow-up interviews conducted years later revealed that boys who had not delayed gratification were described as irritable, while girls were described as sulky. In contrast, boys who had demonstrated patience were described as attentive, and girls were described as competent. Currently, a free self-report tool called the Delaying Gratification Inventory is available online as part of a research project by Central Michigan University. This survey assesses individual differences in the tendency to delay gratification across six specific categories, as well as a global domain. It also provides personalized feedback on this trait, offering insights into one's capacity for deferred gratification.
